This is a small balance remaining to close up the transaction. The contract, inspection, contingencies, &e., amounted to $26,350. This completes the work.
<6839
As a matter of fact, a]] of these are to complete works for which money was voted before ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, in most of these cases ; but 'there may be some works still going on which may require future appropriations.
Quebec-Riviere du LiSvre-reconstruction of dam at Little Rapids, $3,S00.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is a balance necessary to complete a dam. Hon. gentlemen familiar with works of this character know that unless you finish the work you may lose all that has been done.
(Mr. BERGERON. What is the whole amount ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: $20,000 has already been expended, and this balance completes the work.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was it done by contract V

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I am informed that it was a class of work that could not well be done by contract. 1
What are the conditions under which the Dominion government build dams across rivers? I would like to know their general policy in that regard. In our section the party that wants a dam builds it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This was a Dominion work for the improvement of navigation, constructed some years ago at a time when there was a prospect of considerable trade in that region. The work having been constructed as a Dominion work, when disaster came to it, it was necessary for the Dominion to restore it.
What interest had the Dominion in it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The interests of navigation.
What navigation is there on that river ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is practically a small canal. There is a lock there. The work was built as far back as 18SG.

The hon. minister has not given us the principle on which this kind of work is done on the different rivers. There ought to be some principle governing such works. When the government takes the responsibility of damming a river in one locality, I can see no reason why it should not do the same in an another, unless there be some particular reason for the first work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I might have some difficulty in explaining our own principles, but would have much more difficulty in
ioc.^1Dig principles of my predecessor m 1886, by whom this work was constructed. But hon. gentlemen will admit that when the Dominion has spent much money

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: in constructing a public work and then it is damaged, the Dominion should repair it.
I am not talking of this particular work, but generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not voting' works generally, but this particular one.

I do not think that is at all satisfactory. When public works are carried on by the government, there ought to be some general principle on which they proceed, and the government ought to be able to explain it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the improvement of a river in the interests pf navigation would be a wise expenditure ; and while I am not personally acquainted with the work in question, no doubt my predecessor in the late Conservative government believed it would assist trade and commerce in that neighbourhood.
I am glad to see the confidence which the hon. gentleman has in his predecessor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Even if my predecessor put up a work of debatable propriety, we would be expected, when that work is damaged, to repair it. We might have some doubt as to the wisdom of building the Langevin block, but if we found the roof leaking we would consider ourselves bound to repair it.
Does this work serve any good purpose ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was originally constructed because of the probability of considerable traffic in connection with the phosphate trade. At present there is very considerable lumber traffic on that river, there are no railways in its vicinity, there is a considerable settlement in its neighbourhood, and this is the only means the people have of getting access to the market.
No doubt many lumbermen use the river for bringing down logs, do they pay anything to the government ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are no rates charged for the passing of logs, but the use of the lock has been subject to rates.
The policy of the government in the old days was to help to dam rivers, but they made the lumbermen pay tolls sufficient to cover the interest on the expenditure and the cost of keeping the dams.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are slides and dams from which we still get revenue, but this does not come under the same head.
Has there been money expended every year for some years on that work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been some expended on its maintenance.

Sorel, Quebec-Ice piers in River St. Lawrence on west side ot mouth of River Richelieu-revote of $750 lapsed, $3,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The vote of $3,000 in the first instance was insufficient and it was represented that unless further work was ordered, the repairs would he carried away by the pressure. This vote of $3,000 makes the whole amount $6,000.
Has not part of it been carried off by the ice already ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not this season but there was danger of that happening.
When was the original estimate made ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was made before this flood occurred. It was made in the latter part of la03 for the year 1904-5.
It is rather strange that the engineer should not have recognized the possibility of such a thing happening and made his estimates one-half what it should have been.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend has ever undertaken to repair an old house, he must know how difficult it is to estimate the work to be done. As soon as you begin repairing it, you find that other repairs, not originally foreseen, have to be made.
Is this an old job ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not say an old job but an old work.

Where is the line of demarcation between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Marine in some of these items ? The shops at Sorel are in the Marine Department and also a part of the channel, is there not danger of a conflict of jurisdiction ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think an understanding was come to on that point. The shops at Sorel are connected chiefly with the dredging of the ship channel, which is under the Department of Marine and Fisheries. These piers and breakwater have always been under the Department of Public Works.

In Sorel they are also building a beautiful dredge called the 1 W.
S.	Fielding ' for the maritime provinces, which has nothing at all to do with the ship channel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The shops were originally established for the ship channel ; but if they have facilities for work of that character, there is no reason why they should not employ men doing work for any part of the Dominion. The dredge is being built for the Department of Public Works, and will be transferred to it and operated in the same way as other dredges in the maritime provinces.	I

The fact is that the government have been changing their minds too often. Those works were put up at Sorel by the ex-Minister of Public Works, Mr. Tarte. His object was to build dredges which would be used all over the Dominion. It is only since his departure and the advent of the present Minister of Marine, that there has been a change, and the government have since followed a different policy altogether. That is why this government are continuing the work of building dredges there for the maritime provinces. We would have avoided a good deal of the discussion we had the other day concerning dredges in Fort William and Port Arthur, if we had dredges of our own and had not to hire dredges. It was to avoid having to hire dredges that the exMinister of Public Works wanted to build them for the government. And his theory was that the government could, by using their own dredges, have the dredging done for three or four cents per yard instead of forty cents which they have to pay when they hire other dredges. There seems to be a scarcity of dredges in the country or if there are any dredges they are in the hands of the government and it is no use for any one else to tender. It was to avoid that, as I remember the explanation given by Mr. Tarte in this House, that he wanted to build dredges belonging to the government that could do the work for which we pay 40 cents or 50 cents for 3 cents or 4 cents. It was accepted at that time by the government as good policy, but now it has been abandoned and that is why we are informed that the shops at Sorel are to build dredges only for the ship channel.
River Maskinonge-dredging, $3,800.
Does the government own this dredge ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, this is being done by a private dredge owned by Mr. St. Pierre. This dredge was employed at $7 per hour, the rate established some years ago.
Have they lots of work to do there yet ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This I understand, closes up the contract for the arrangement, it was not a contract, with this gentleman and tenders are being taken for the work on the basis of so much a yard.
Is it navigable ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I am so informed.
Is it cheaper to give so much per yard or to pay $7 an hour ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is always a matter of debate in the House. The department is no longer following the system of hiring dredges by the hour, but are fixing a price per cubic yard.

I am glad to hear the department are going to drop the system of hiring dredges by the hour, that is if they have a proper system of measuring the number of yards of earth taken out. I know that from an experience that took place in my own country where a dredge was hired during 1903-4. One stipulation was that the dredge was to take out at least 1,000 yards of earth for 12 hours so that the dredge when it took out 1,000 yards stopped its work for the day, although it is a notorious fact that it could take out
3.000	yards as easily as 1,000. It seems to me to be ridiculous to hire a dredge stipulating to take out 1,000 yards knowing that that same dredge.has a capacity of three times that amount per day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The officers inform me it is the practice of the department in hiring by the hour to stipulate that the dredges shall take out a certain quantity a day, and if they take out that quantity they presume their day's work is ended.
Mr. LALOIi. I have affidavits in my possession, and I shall probably take up the matter again, showing that in the case of a dredge employed in the Grand river at Dunnvi.lle, the contract with the government stipulated that it should take out
1.000	yards a day, and I have affidavits that the captain informed the men on the dredge and the tug men to take it easy and not hurry, because all they had to do was to take out 1,000 yards, whereas it is a notorious fact that the dredge has taken out
1.000	yards before noon and done nothing more for the rest of the day. I think the payment should be regulated by the kind of dredging and where they can take out more than 1,000 yards, I cannot see why it should be stopped at a thousand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In such a case I suppose we would have to pay a larger rate per hour, but if the contract stipulated that they should perform 1,000 yards of dredging a day and the dredge did that amount I suppose we could hardly expect the dredging contractor to do a lot more work for nothing. Whether or not $7 an hour is a fair price is another matter. The contract only called for 1,000 yards a day. There is nothing wrong then in the dredge only doing 1,000 yards a day.

I do not quite agree with the minister. As I stated there are different kinds of dredging. Where the excavating is easy and the dredge is being paid $12 an hour and they can take out 3,000 in place of 1,000 I do not see why they Mr. FIELDING.
should not be compelled to work for the 12 hours at their full capacity and take out as much as possible. I do not see why they should be allowed to drag the job along week after week, when they cou'.d by working at their full capacity do it in one-third the time.
Yes.	.

And they stop when the 1,000 yards is done ? I would think that is very poor business management. I could readily understand that an arrangement might be made so that a dredge should take out at least so much per day, but to say that a dredge is to be hired at so much an hour for 12 hours and be paid for 12 hours even if it works only half that time, seems to me is not very good business management.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The difficulty I see is that if you have a dredge by the hour and you have an inspector to see that the dredge is not loafing and you put in a stipulation that you are to pay them by the hour for 12 hours a day if they take out a certain quantity, although they may do it in 2 hours they are paid for the 12 hours.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend see that if there was no such regulation the dredge might put in the time loafing and take out much less ? The stipulation of 1,000 yards is in the public interest, that they should at all events give a fair day's work. The only possible room for criticism is that the dredge might have been able to do more work and should be allowed to get more pay.

Does not the minister see that is the minimum amount of dredg-

ing to be done under the most disadvantageous circumstances and they must do that under any circumstances. That would be a reasonable business proposition it seems to me. But, to say that after they have taken out a eertan quantity, payment goes on whether they work or not, does not seem to me to be a good arrangement to make with the owners of the dredges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The method of dealing with these matters is changed now, so that in discussing this we are discussing a matter of the past. But I cannot see that if the quantity stipulated has been taken out, the sum stipulated should not be paid. My own observation is that men working either for the government or for private employers are not disposed to do more than they are paid for.
Then it seems to me that the better plan would be to pay so much per cubic yard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what is being done.

There is another point. Every one knows that the quantity of material a dredge can take out depends upon the character of that material. I understand that the limit fixed is simply the minimum quantity that they are to take out, whatever the character of the material. But to say that because they happen to have easy work they should stop when they have taken out the quantity fixed as a minimum is an entire misconstruction of the understanding.

If I understand it correctly, the dredge is paid according to her capacity -the more work she can do the higher the pay. To say that a dredge could get $12 per hour is all right. But that should mean that in the hardest kind of dredging they could encounter they should be able to take out at least 1,000 yards. What I cannot understand is fixing the minimum at 1,000 yards where the material is such that the dredge could do three times that amount. The dredge is hired to work for twelve hours a day, and she should work to her capacity for twelve hours under proper inspection to earn a day's pay, regardless of how great a quantity she takes out.
IMr. FIELDING. As the system now adopted is to pay by the cubic yard, we are really discussing a past transaction. But if the quantity taken out is fixed at 1,000 yards, the price might be satisfactory ; but, on that basis, if the dredge were obliged to take out more, the price would not be satisfactory. This was practically a system of piece work, and the sum paid per hour was the result of a calculation of a certain number of cents per cubic yard, which was regarded as a fair price for the work. That being the case, if a dredge.took up more, her
owners would expect to be paid accordingly. It all comes to a question of what is a fair price for removing the material.
The hon. minister does not intend to say that for all kinds of dredging the dredge will do the same amount of work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
This minimum was fixed, as I understand it, on the basis of the hardest digging-the dredge must not do less, but if the material were favourable it might do more.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed by the officers of the department that this minimum did not contemplate the hardest kind of digging, but ordinary digging. But this has been done away with. The system adopted is that of paying by the cubic yard, which is a better system.
Does not the same price apply to all ? I see that the price paid in Ontario is $8 per hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The price varies according to the capacity of the dredge.
There seems to be quite a uniformity of price all over Canada. Am I to understand that it runs from $7 to $12 an hour ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes ; that is correct.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
That is on the basis of
1,000	yards ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No ; the value of the dredge would depend upon her capacity.
What is the limit where you pay $7 or $8 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The quality was not the same for all dredges. It was based upon a fair price per cubic yard.

That is, the maximum would be 1,000 yards a day, no matter how long it took to move the earth. In the report of the Minister of Public Works dealing with the different dredges, I find that the minister gives the cost per cubic yard as 5i cents, 4 cents and as low as 3 cents per cubic yard. This dredge was given $84 per day when the contract could probably have been made for $40 or $50 based upon the amount of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No ; the very favourable rates the hon. gentleman quotes are those of the powerful dredges of the government. But ordinary dredges do not do the work at that price. It all shows the wisdom of getting more government dredges.	,

That is the proper policy for this government-to build its own dredges. I understand that Hon. Mr. Tarte, when Minister of Public Works, stated that the work could be done with government

dredges for from 3 cents to 4 cents per cubic yard. I cannot understand, then, why Mr. Conmee, Mr. Boone, Mr. Bowman and others should get these enormous prices when the government, with their command of cajpitai, can build dredges that will do the work so much cheaper.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree that the construction of government dredges is the best policy, and the hon. gentleman will see that the government is making progress along that line. As to the maritime provinces, I shall be very glad to find some one there with dredges, no matter what his politics, to do the work waiting to be done. My hon. friends from Ontario are fortunate in having private dredges that can do the work. When we try to get dredges for work in the maritime provinces we are told that the dredges are busy and we cannot have them.

If the minister will not regard politics, but will give contracts in the maritime provinces on the same basis as these contracts are given to Mr. Conmee and Mr. Bowman and some others, I do not doubt that we can quickly form a company to build a dredge and take a contract. But we will want assurance that we shall not be required to change our politics to get fair-play.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will promise my bon. friend (Mr. Lalor) that if be will tender for a contract in the maritime provinces any where that comes within what I may call my sphere of influence, the lowest tenderer will get the contract no matter what his polities.
But if there were any chance of some of us tendering, I suppose the hon. minister would insert the advertisement on Saturday and provide that tenders were to be in on Monday morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No ; we will give you a fair chance.
Public Works-chargeable to income-River Chateauguay - dredging, revote of lapsed amount, $1,850.
Who is doing that work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Canadian Construction Company. This is work in Chateauguay basin, in the mouth of the Chateauguay river. This is money that was designed to be spent on that work, but they were. not able to spend it in 1903-4. This is needed to complete the contract.
Is that dredge working by the hour or by the yard ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This dredge was at that time working by the hour. There is no work going on now at all. The work is done. The work upon which she has been engaged is stopped and tenders are being called for further work of the same class.

I want to call the attention of the hon. Acting Minister of Public Works to this work. I do not object at all to this work ; in fact, if I remember well I asked for the work some years ago. But, the money that is being spent there to-day is being uselessly spent. The engineer, I am sure, will bear me out when I say that they are working in what is called quicksand. They have been working there for the last fifteen or sixteen years and the channel is filling up all the time. I have seen the dredge there myself very often and I have no doubt they will have to keep up the same work every year and with no good result. The pilot on one of the boats that passes there told me that in order to establish a permanent work which would stand for a long time, it would be necessary to construct crib-work to protect the channel and keep the sand from filling in. That has been done at Ste. Anne's for the same purpose, the material there being quicksand. It may cost a little more at the outset but the work *would be of a permanent character. The department are spending $5,000 or $6,000 a year in dredging the river Chateauguay and no good result is being accomplished. The work will have to be done year after year because the channel will fill up, on account of the nature of the material. I call the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance, who is the custodian of our money, to the condition of this work and I also call the attention of the department to it. I am sure the engineer must know that part of the river. He was there himself years ago and he knows that what I am speaking of should be done if he wants to put a stop to the expense, which is not objectionable in itself, but which is not producing the desired result on account of the unwise policy which has been pursued in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend has been misinformed and that he is confusing some other class of work with this, because I find by the memorandum which has been supplied to me that this dredging is described as being for the purpose of removing hard-pan, boulders and clay.

There are two places where they have been working. One of these is in the River Chateauguay where they have taken awray stones. The other place that I am talking of is at -the mouth of the River Chateauguay or just above the river where a channel is being made for boats coming from the lake into the river.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend -will probably find on inquiry that he is mistaken, and that there is no work being done at the place he indicates. This work is for the removal of hard-pan, boulders and clay. There is sand iu the river but these operations are not in the sand district at all.

Last year there was a dredge at the mouth of the river working

In the sand and there was another one down the river. They have been working at three or four places in the river.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that the sand is not at the mouth of the river.

Well it is. I am very sorry that the engineer does not remember. There is a sand bank at the head of the River Chateauguay. Steamers passing there have to go around nearly a mile to avoid that bank. The government years ago commenced work in the channel. They have been working at that since. They were working at that last summer. I have seen the dredge at work there. It is that gap that is filling uip all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no question that the dredge has been working during the past season at the mouth of the river, not at the head of the river. 1 am told that the sand to which my hon. friend refers is not at this point.
It is at two places.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been work done at both places undoubtedly, but the work to which this appropriation refers was not in the sand but in the harder material at the mouth of the river.

That may be, because they were working at the lower' end of the river and they were working also at the entrance to the river or above Nun's Island. Whether this amount of money is specially for that work or not I want to call the attention of the hon. minister to the fact that in order to make a good work at the entrance to the river it should be done in a different way from that in which it is being carried out now.
Doucet's Lauding-dredging, $8,000.
Is this done by tender or ir. what way ? It is a very large item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This was done by the old system of per hour.
What is this ?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This is in the county of Nicolet. It is opposite Three Rivers. It is the terminus of the Grand Trunk branch line from Athabaska to Doucet's Landing and there are two boats plying between Three Rivers and Doucet's Landing. It is a very important terminus ; in fact it is the only important connection between the north and south shores at that point.
What was the amount of money voted last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: $12,000 was appropriated in the estimates for the current year. That has all been expended and this further sum is needed.
That will make $20.000 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
What is the capacity of the dredge there ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The cost of removing the material is 13 8-10 cents per cubic yard.
How is it that there is so much difference between the appropriation and the actual amount ? You have $12,000 and $8,000, making altogether $20,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, they found that the amount was insufficient to make the work effective and they require to make a further expenditure. This is practically a portion of the harbour of Three Rivers.
No, it is on the other side from Three Rivers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, it is the approach to the harbour of Three Rivers and it has proved of great value to. the commerce of Three Rivers.

It is on the south side of the river. When a department comes to council and asks for some money is the hon. Minister of Finance not anxious to know why these appropriations should not be made in a better way than that ? Who makes the valuation of such a work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is made by the engineers of the Public Works Department.
They make a valuation at $12,000 and spend $20,000. That should strike the mind of my hon. friend when the department come to him for money and when he comes to parliament and asks for a vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I was told by the owner of the dredges which worked there last year that the bottom of the river is very sandy, and that the new harbour work at Three Rivers had caused the sand to silt over on to the other side. The river is narrow there and there are battures. The people were threatened by the navigation company that if the work was not done the boat service would cease.
The proposal is to excavate 800 feet in length and 400 feet in width. IIow much of that work has been done and how much is there to complete ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The quantity already removed as covered by this appropriation is 144,456 cubic yards and about 100,000 yards remain to be done.
Then, about two-fifths of the work has been done at an expense of about $20,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a contract for any specific amount of work.
Do I understand that new tenders are to be called for the balance of the work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Tenders have been called for the dredging.
Under the old arrangement $20,000 were expended and now you propose to continue the same work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
At what cost ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are $15,000 in the main estimates for the coming year.
Have tenders been received ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but the contract has not yet been awarded.
When you have expended this $35,000 in all, will the sand continue to silt in there and will you have to renew the dredging every year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is expected that the work will be good in the main.
, Will the sand not continue to drift over from the Three Rivers side ?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
According to the report prepared by the resident engineer at lhy request that will be provided against. The plan is to deepen the channel for the boats that ply between Three Rivers and Doucet's Landing, and they will build a wharf on the south east of the existing wharf which is the property of the Grand Trunk and which at present is in a complete state of decay.
River St. Maurice-dredging, $11,200.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The appropriation taken for this work was only $6,000, but Strong pressure was brought to make provision for more expensive work and an additional appropriation is being asked. Considering that the appropriation was only $6,000 originally the additional sum is out of reasonable proportion, but the department informs me that the reasons were very urgent and the public opinion in the district pressed the department to do a larger amount of work.
Is that river navigable at that point ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are very large saw mill operations going on there.
Do the lumbermen contribute anything to this work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The lumbermen pay fees on slides and booms which are a considerable source of revenue.
That is another matter altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Dredging and work of that character would not be done by the lumbermen.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: During the last five years two large lumber companies have established themselves at the mouth of the river and employ about 1,000 people.

I am merely asking for information as to why this money should be voted, and the statement of my hon. friend leads me to believe that the river there is navigated by tugs and barges carrying pulp wood.
This river has been on the pay roll for many years ; are we to continue year after year dredging it out ?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is one of the three largest rivers in the Dominion and it is the river par excellence of the lumber trade in the province of Quebec. Within the last few years large limits have been sold by the Quebec government and several American firms have established themselves there.
Montmorency-wharf improvements, $2,500.
Is this a new work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a new work, and this balance of $2,500 will finish it.
It is described here as improving a wharf ; if it is a new wharf what do you want improving it for ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed there was an old wharf there, but this is practically a new work.
There were a great many promises made there last election ; are you redeeming your promises now ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean in the county of Montmorency 1
Yes, Sir.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But this is in the county of Quebec.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This place is in the county of Quebec, not in Montmorency. It is between Chateau Richard and Beauport.
It must be at the Falls, and I do not think there is any need of a wharf there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Will it be completed this year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, iu the coming fiscal year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was the work let by tender ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It was done during election time by day labour. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no election in the summer, when this was done.
How is it that the government are departing from the policy they are supposed to have of letting these works by tender ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This was done by day labour for reasons which the department felt were good.
I think the committee are entitled to know what those reasons were.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I may inform my hon. friend that in my experience in the county of Gaspe many- wharfs and breakwaters have been built in recent years by day's work at much less than they were tendered for. Although the government have adopted the policy of giving contracts where the amount exceeds $5,000, yet nothing prevents the department from proceeding by' day's work. In the present instance, they proceeded by day's work before this law was passed. I can cite cases iu the county of Gaspd where the amount estimated by the department was doubled and trebled when tenders were called for, and they had to revert to day's work.

Surely some one would be responsible for that. Do I understand my hon. friend to say that after an engineer has made an estimate and the department has then received tenders, they doubled and trebled the estimate ?
Mr. LEMIE'UX. Yes, and the department in those cases have refused to give the contract.

In cases where they have refused to give a contract and have done the work by day's work, has it cost less or more than the estimate made by the engineer ? A competent engineer ought to know pretty nearly what a work will cost.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: To my knowledge the cost by day's work has not exceeded the estimate of the engineer, while in some cases work done by contract has exceeded tne estimate.

Do I understand that the cost of work done by day's work
has come within the estimate of the engineer, while in many cases the tenders have been away above the estimate ? That seems extraordinary.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It has happened many a time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That may be accounted for by the works not having been sufficiently advertised. If you have allowed only a few days, anticipating that certain men would tender, they might easily go away above the estimate, hoping to get the work without competition ; but in ordinary cases,
I do not think there would be that difference.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I could cite cases in the county of Gaspe. As to the notices of tenders, my hon. friend may find them every day in the papers, and he will see that some thirty days are allowed.

The examples given by my hon. friend from Nlcolet cannot be got everywhere. The county of Gaspe is far away, and the contractors cannot very well take their plant down there. The case under discussion is near Quebec, and the circumstances are quite different. It seems to me that when we have a law on this point, the government should observe it. and that every work costing over $5,000 should be done by contract. I have seen a good many works done by the day, and they are always very costly ; and it seems to me that it would be a great deal better for the government to observe the law. This $2,500 we are now voting has been spent and the amount in the main estimates to be voted is $6,000, so the total will be nearly $9,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: That is another reason why the work should be given by tender. It is near the city of Quebec and there are contractors in Quebec.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They are very busy now.
What was the saving effected between the amount of the lowest tender and the actual cost ?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Let me give an example to my hon. friend. Last year we called for tenders to build a breakwater in Mal-baie in the county of Gaspe. There weie five or six tenders, the lowest of wliirh was $40,000, while the estimate of the chief engineer was only $20,000. The minister did not feel justified in giving the contract to the lowest tenderer, so the work was started by day labour and the resident engineer pays he will be able to keep within the chief engineer's estimate. I could gi've many other examples, speaking of my own county. No doubt the contractors are afraid of the distance and the cost of transport of the plant and men, and that is why they

raise their prices ; hut it has been the linvariable experience I have .had in connection with those works in my county, that the system of doing the work by day labour, without contract, is the cheaper.

Will the hon. minister tell us why Conservatives are never employed on these works ? This system of having the government work done without contract is but another way of evading the election law, because they employ nobody but Grits.
Mr. LKiMIEUX. I can tell my hon. friend that whenever work is done in the county of Gaspe the resident engineer appoints a local inspector, and I have invariably told the local inspector to employ both parties because it is public expenditure and both parties should be given work.

Let me draw attention to the condition of affairs in my county. We have there a Welland canal feeder, and the men who work on it are not engaged by either the superintendent or the deputy superintendent of the canal. If a labouring man wants employment on any government work there, he must run the gauntlet of the Liberal Association. His name is brought before the association ; and if acceptable, he is given an order on the deputy superintendent, which entitles him to be employed. Recently a most respectable man, who had been working on the Welland canal feeder for the last 25 years, and who has raised a fine family very much respected in the community, was suspected of having voted for me at the last election, and consequently, when the work was opened as usual, was refused employment. A friend of his called the attention of the president of the Liberal Association to the fact, and the reply was : He voted for Lalor ; he had better go to Lalor to get work. That man has not got one hours' work in Dunnville this year simply because he is suspected of having voted for me. It is most disgraceful that a labouring man should not be able to get work at $1.25 a day shovelling stone or earth for the government without having to run the gauntlet of the Liberal Association or committee and getting its approval. I am a large employer of labour. I have a number of factories and other institutions where I employ labour to a large extent, but there never was a time when I would stoop to compel an ordinary working man to vote for me in order that he might get work. We have, however, the government setting this example to the employers of labour and inducing them to take means to make the labouring man vote their ticket. That is certainly a disgraceful state of affairs. It is all very well to use political influence, but it is disgraceful, on the part of any government to stoop so low- as to eom-Mr. LEMIEUX.
pel labouring men to vote for it in order that they may obtain work.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The. hon. minister has stated that this work is going to cost $11,000 when finished. He asked $3,000 in the main estimates last year, this supplementary vote of $2,500 is to complete last year's work, and he will ask $6,000 next year. What does he propose to do with the Act respecting Public Works ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Act will have to be obeyed.
It has been the law since 1886 that any new work involving an expenditux-e exceeding $5,000 can only be let after calling for tenders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the appropriation was taken, there was only to he an expenditure of $4,000 so that that work would not come within the rule.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend knew before starting the work that it was going to cost more than $4,000, because he has already spent more than $5,500 this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was an estimate originally for the work, but when this appropriation was taken the department could only make its contract for the $4,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is not the way. Hon. gentlemen come down hero with an estimate say to start a post office, to buy a site, get the plans and let the tenders and get say $4,000 to pay dux-ing the first year no matter whether the cost is to be $30,000 or $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the usual practice.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why was it not carried out here ? There was evidently a job as my hon. friend beside me suggests ; a lot of promises were made and they were carried out at election time and this $2,500 is to pay a balance not provided for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is nice to have my hon. friend say that promises were carried out. Generally the complaint is the other way. As to why the minister of the day did not treat this as a matter of contract, I cannot definitely answer, but this I can say that the engineers assure me the work performed has been well done and we have fair value for the money. There is no job, no extravagance and we have good value for the money.

I wish to say a word in support of what my hon. friend from Haldi-mand has said with regard to men employed by the government. I certainly think that if there is a vacant position of any great value it is only right and fair that the government should appoint a man with the same leanings as they have. That is a reasonable thing provided he is a good man. I take no exception to that what-

ever, but I certainly do not think that the ordinary labouring man should be employed or not employed by the government according to his political leanings. It seems to me that if we are going to have a free country here, men should be allowed to exercise their franchise as they see fit, and as long as they do not take an active part in politics and make themselves offensive, government employees should be allowed to vote as they like and that they should not be asked to which side they belong before they are employed for a day's work. Dike the hon. member for Haldimand I am a large employer of labour myself, and I have never yet nor will I ask a man his politics before I employ him. It is a most unfair, unreasonable and unjust question to put to any man. I have here an afiidavit which X shall read to the House :
Province of Quebec, County of Argentuil.
I, Hilaire Robillard, of the village of Carillon, in the electoral distriot of Argenteuil, do solemnly declare that for some time before, and up to the second day of November last, I had been in the employ of the federal government in charge of a gang of men working on a pier being built in the Ottawa river in the vicinity of the village of Carillon. On the day before polling, in November last, I was informed by Mr. Girard, who was supervising the construction of said pier, that my services were no longer required, no reason being assigned for such action, and I was replaced by another workman. Some time previous to my dismissal I was told by Mr. Girard that any person working for the government would be expected to vote for the party in power. I was at that time and am still a parliamentary elector, and I attended two political meetings in Carillon before the election. My political sympathies were suspected, as I did not give the assurances expected of me, and I heard divers rumours that I was going to be dismissed on account of my politics, or for political reasons. Beyond exercising my electoral franchise I took no part, nor did X participate in said election. Although I am a poor and illiterate man, I always understood that Canada was a free country, and did not exist in the exclusive interest of any political party. And I make this solemn declaration, conscientiously believing the same to be true, and knowing it to be of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Declared before me at the village of Carillon this 14th day of March, A.D. 1905.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Justice of the Peace.
I think it is only fair and reasonable, as I said before, when there is a vacant postmastership or office of any kind in the Department of Public Works or of Railways and Canals that a person of the political stripe of the government in power should be employed, but beyond that it seems to me to be wrong for the government to go, and most unfair. I do not know which department this was in. Public Works or Railways and Canals, but it does not matter. This question has come 218
up before and it seems to me a very important one. I certainly would like to get some assurance from the government that they do not expect or will not allow their officers to bring pressure on the ordinary servants and employees of the government to vote for the party in power as if the power in power were entitled to their votes simply because the government give them work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I believe that the matters referred to both by my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) and my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) belong to the Department of Railways and Canals, and I have no desire to discuss the affairs of that department, but so far as the principles involved are concerned I have no hesitation in giving my opinion at once. I notice that tihis poor illiterate man has made somewhat of a political document of his affidavit and it strikes me if the man himself had no interest in politics somebody who framed the affidavit for him bad a good deal of interest, because a poor illiterate mail of bis own motion would not make such an affidavit as that. If the affidavit says that any man, high or low, in the service of the government was dismissed from his labour because he exercised his franchise freely and independently, I do not hesitate to say that is wrong. Any attempt to interfere with the free exercise of the franchise by any officer or servant, I would condemn as strongly as my hon. friends. I would not encourage the idea of a Dominion official taking an active part in politics. If he takes no active part but exercises his franchise I say that whether he occupies the position of lieutenant governor or labourer, that is his right and should not be interfered with, and if any man was dismissed because of his vote, that I would condemn, but I would like to have the facts more clearly investigated. As to the general principle so long as we have the principle of party government in Canada, I fancy we will have the same discussion as we have had to-day. The party system seems to have its advantages and its disadvantages, but on the whole it seems to he the best way of working out constitutional government in the British empire. We must take the good and the evil together and one of the evils is that this question of political partisanship always comes up. Just how my hon. friend would draw the distinction between labouring men and men in higher ranks I do not understand. Are we to be told that a man who aspires to a high office can say : ' I am your friend, I have helped you, and I think when a vacancy occurs I should be considered.' But the poor labouring man who uses such an argument is told it is all wrong. If it is legitimate for a man who wants to be a judge or an engineer or to occupy any higher position to come and say : ' I have helped your party in an honourable way, I have supported you and as-



sisted you and want to be considered,' why should not that argument be equally good for the poor labouring man ? I cannot see Any difference, such as my hon. friend would *irge. I have no doubt hundreds of thousands of Conservatives have been employed all over the country on various public works. Iii my own province I know cases that have come within my own observation where the work was given indiscriminately. I would not desire otherwise, but if a choice is made, if there is to be a preference of A to B what ground of complaint is there so long as A is competent to do a good day's work ? Why should there not *be as much liberty to give a preference to a poor labouring man as to a lawyer who wants to be a judge ?	1 cannot see the
distinction. All the interest the public has is to see that a man is not dismissed for the free exercise of the franchise, and that no man is told he cannot vote one way or the other in order to hold his place, and 'lastly that the work is well done at a fair *day's wage. What other interest have the public in the matter ? I cannot see any ground for my hon. friend's grievances.
It seems to me that most of the minister's remarks do not apply to the question under discussion. This man was in the employ of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I accept that. If he was dismissed on account of his vote, I say it was wrong.

But . the minister will iknow how hard it is to prove a thing of that kind. It is a matter of common report in that section that not only this man, but six or seven others, were dismissed for that reason ; they went to a political meeting, and even had the audacity to applaud the Conservative candidate ; and, within the next few days, they were dismissed. Of *course, it is hard to prove any connection between these two things. The hon. minister says something about the wording of the affidavit. No doubt the man went to a lawyer, as any of us would, and the lawyer drew up the affidavit according to the facts as stated. That affidavit, it seems to me, is as near proof as can be expected in a case *of this kind. I believe the matter should be fully considered, and that the officers who have taken such action should be warned not to repeat it.

I agree that when a government office of emolument is open it is only to be expected that the man who has worked for his party should be given the preference in the appointment. That is party government, and it is conceded to be the proper system for this country. But when It comes to employing ordinary labouring-men, the position is entirely different. We should consider it a great hardship if ordinary employers of labour were to give or refuse employment according to a man's poli-Mr. FIELDING.
tics. I think it is very wrong for the government to set an example of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Lalor) that even though au employee of the government votes against the government, to dismiss him on that account would be an outrage.

But that is particularly true in the case of an honest, conscientious labouring man employed upon a public work. I can tell the bon. minister, and prove it beyond a doubt, that a man who wishes work on the Grand river feeder at Dunnville has to run the gauntlet of the Liberal Association committee before he can get work. He gets the order of that committee to the superintendent to engage him. But if he lias voted for Lalor, or is even suspected of having done so, employment Is refused him. I have in mind the case of one man, a worthy man, one who has raised a family that is respected by everybody. When he applied for employment he was told that he had voted for Lalor and so could not be given work. I say that principle is radically wrong, and the minister who is in charge of the department should issue a specific order to the officer in charge of this work stating- that men are to be employed regardless of politics, so long as they are good men. The minister must know that it adds immensely to the difficulty of getting good men for these public works if the superintendent is not allowed to exercise his own judgment, but must consider politics in making his selection. I know that men who are almost worthless are engaged on public works because they are supposed to vote for the government. We do not get the worth of our money from the labour of these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Lalor) has confused two different things. I agree with him in one, but not in the other. One is the question of the dismissal of a public officer because of bis vote, and the other is the question of exercising a political preference in filling a vacancy in the public service. If a man is in the public service, having got there under the Conservative regime, we assume that be got there honourably and is there by right, and there should be no interference with his right to vote as he pleases. In my own department I have men who were appointed before my day, and I never interfere with them, nor would I allow them to be interfered with, in voting as they please. But when it comes to the filling of a vacancy. I have a right to consider the politics of the applicant, provided always that I put in none but good men. But why the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lalor) should draw a distinction between the employment by the government of a labouring man and any other man, I do not understand. A private employer would not make that distinction-whatever the position to be filled, be would not con-

sider the politics of the applicant. If he wished to engage a lawyer, he would not consider whether that lawyer was a Grit or a Tory. But is the labouring man who has done good service for his party to be put upon a different plane from any other ? Why should he not be as much entitled to have a preference in a vacancy that he can fill as the lawyer who wishes to be a judge ?
With the minister's permission, I will correct him on that point. It is not a question of engaging a man, but a question whether a man must change his politics in order to get employment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be the case m the highly paid offices as well as in any other, and my hon. friend (Mr. Lalor) sees nothing wrong in political patronage in an office that carries a good salary. I myself justify that, always provided that capable men are employed. The hon. gentleman says that in the case he refers to inefficient men are employed. I say that is wrong ; no engineer should be asked to employ men on a public work who are not capable I do not hesitate to say that this is a matter that I had hoped would not arise. I have endeavoured to see that the Conservatives as well as Liberals get a fan- share of work. But if it were put to me : Here is a vacancy for a labouring man and here are two men applying, one a Grit and one a Tory, and both good men, I would support the Grit, just as my hon. friend would prefer the Tory.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend from Ilal-dimand (Mr. Lalor) did not put it in that way. My hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Morin) referred to this work going on at Montmorency, for the performance of which the government asked $4,000. And they have spent $6,000 already and are asking for $o,000 to complete the work. They have done this work by day labour, yet a man who votes Conservative cannot get a dollar of that work. Is that fair ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I desire to be perfectly frank with my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor). If I were in Quebec and in that district, and twenty men were wanted on that work, and twenty Liberals and twenty Conservatives applied, all good men, I would give the preference to the Liberals, and I would not think I was doing wrong. And I frankly say that I would expect the hon. gentleman, if his party were in power and the matter were within his sphere of influence, to give his preference to the Conservatives.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Then the hon. minister would not show himself a good business man. This government professes to be a business government; yet, if you take the employers of this country, I venture to say you cannot find one who, employing men to do labour, asks what the applicant's politics are. Here is work on which the government are spending over $11,000 contrary to
218i
the law, and yet no labouring man who happens to be a Conservative can get a day's work on that job, no matter how hard up he may be. No manufacturer would carry on his business in that way. I have men in my own employ who turn out and work against me at every election. They are good men, and they have a right to do as they please. I employ a large number of men, and I never inquire of any of them what side he voted for or what his religion was. And the government ought to do the same. I would like to ask the hon. minister how much the engineer's estimate for this work was when it was originally brought down ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The engineer informs me that it was $9,000, if he remembers correctly. I do not want to get involved in two distinct questions. As to the value of the work and whether too much money was expended on it or not, I think, that is a proper question. But we have for the last few minutes been discussing not that question but the general principle involved in giving a political preference to one's own political friends. In private affairs you do not do that because private affairs are not conducted on the party system, but I venture to say that my hon. friend's friends in the province of Ontario will give a political preference to their own friends, they will have a perfect right to do so, and if they are attacked for it I will be one to say that they have a perfect right to give a preference to their own friends whether it be a matter of day's labour or the appointment of a high officer, always provided they appoint a man capable of doing the work and of giving an honest day's work for an honest day's pay.

The hon. Minister of Finance did not follow the instructions given to him and to the country by the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Here in 1896 the right hon. leader of tlie government said that where men were working for the government it made no difference whether they were Grits or Tories they should not be removed. He said that all men would have the right to vote the way they chose and that they would not be interfered with. Contrast that with the example we had in 1900 when Mr. Blair wrote to the manager of the Soulanges canal and said to him :	Have you any men in your
employ who voted for Bergeron ? If you have, turn them all out. This is the very man and that letter was read in this House.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This canal is not in the constituency of my hon. friend from Beau-harnois (Mr. Bergeron). It is on the other side of the river.
What is the difference so long as they work on the canal ?
Many of them work on both sides.

Are those the instructions given by the leader of the government ? Not
at all I wish the hon. Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) were here to-day. I would give him another example. Last year I asked him for a post office to be granted at Detroit where 500 people would he served. But no, I was refused because I was a lory. Since then he has opened up two new post offices and probably from ten to twenty people will be served by these post offices. That is the way the other side of the House carries out the instructions of the leadei of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Misery loves company.
I am in very good company on that question.
I applied to my hon. friend the Postmaster General a short time ago to put a post office in a certain place in my own province but l regret to say that he refused to do it. So, 1 can sympathize with my hon. friend (Mi. Morin). We are both in the same box. \\ e have both been treated in the same way by this hard hearted gentleman.
. Mr. LALOR. It was time to strike.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I suppose that what, the hon. gentleman refers to was the bolt, but I believe that at the time of the bolt they were not able to do any business. As to the other question I think my hon. friend must be mistaken about that letter ot Mr. Blair I have no recollection of ever having heard a letter of the character which my hon. friend states from Mr. Blair read m this House. If there was such a letter it was a most extraordinary one. I would like to hear from Mr. Blair on the question, but I do not think that he ever wrote any such letter as that. Certainly I would not defend any such letter. I think there must be some mistake.

I have a much worse complaint to make against the hon. Postmaster General than that of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin) and the hon. Minister of Finance. In my riding a postmaster applied for an increase of his salary. I made application on his behalf. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) looked up to see what was the revenue ot the office and he reduced his salary notwithstanding the fact that the postmastei was a good Grit.
I would like to ask hon. gentlemen opposite if it is not a fact^ that the Whitney government have been discharging officials in the province of Ontario right and left.

If the Whitney government follow the course pursued by hon. gentlemen oppposite during the last ten years _ there will be very few Grits left in office m the province of Ontario. We know that during the last ten years no government in the world has discharged as many officials on account of their political leanings as the present government has done. We have this going on all over. They are weeding them

out every year by the hundreds, and I car. assure you that there is only a very small remnant of Conservative officers left m tne province of Ontario, and I presume that the state of affairs in other provinces is just as bad as it is in Ontario. As far as the Ontario government are concerned they have kept their hands off the officials unless there was cause. I challenge anybody to show where there has been a single official in the province of Ontario discharged by the Whitney government since they came into power without cause.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same here.

I venture to say that there is a large number of officials in Ontario to-day, who, if they have not been discharged ought to have been. They took a very active part in the last campaign. They appeared on the platform and engaged in active politics in other ways. They adhered to the Reform government and did everything m then power to defeat the Conservative candidates. We have to-day for the first time in the Dominion of Canada the spectacle of the hon. Minister of Finance getting up in his place and openly and boldly declaring that to the victor belongs the spoils. That is the position he has taken and he has told us that if there are men to be found that will do the work it should be given to Grits and Conservatives should not be employed. I venture to say that the object of such a statement is to give notice to those who are employing men on public works throughout this Dominion that it is the wish of the present government that they shall .employ Grits.
I say it is an extraordinary course to pursue yet we have had this principle proclaimed here in this House I think probably for the first time, although it has been acted upon on every possible occasion. We do know that even away down to the working men down to those employed on the public works they extend this principle, that they watch these men very closely that they choose their own political friends and that they dismiss men by the hundreds all over the Dominion where they find that at the last election they in any way showed their preference for the Conservative candidate. I think this is a very serious state of affairs, and I think that even Reformers for then-own sake should pursue a somewhat milder course. The words uttered by the hon. Minister of Finance will echo and re-echo throughout this Dominion, and I have no doubt that the Conservative friends of Mr. Whitney will point to these words and will say : Here we have the announcement from the Minister of Finance that this government are carrying out the spoils system, and that where Tories are found to be employed on a government work in the most humble positions if they can obtain Reformers they will discharge them because they are not going to employ Conservatives. That is the position that has been taken here

to-day and I venture to say again that if the Reformers were to be treated in the province of Ontario the same as the Conservatives have been all through this Dominion it would he very much worse for them. Whatever justification the Whitney government may have I hope they will not follow the example of the present government to the extent they have in weeding out their opponents ; in fact, I hope no man in Ontario will ever be disturbed in so far as the provincial government are concerned on account of his political leanings, and I hope the time will never come that they will get down to the position of asking a man what his political leanings are when he is asking for employment on a public work for which the people and not the government have to pay.
It seems to me that this is a declaration which is dangerous to the public weal and it will be acted upon as doubtless it was intended to be by the friends of the government. Notwithstanding that the strongest plank in the Liberal platform was that good officials would not be interfered with, and notwithstanding that they denounced the Conservatives, for ten years the Liberal government has been decapitating Conservative officials. Then, that safety valve which we supposed existed requiring that contracts over $5,000 should be let by public tender ; that has disappeared under the present government. They must know from their engineers what a work will cost before they undertake it, but their policy is 'to come down to parliament the first year asking for a vote under $5,000, then let the work without competition, and then come back next session asking for another vote of several thousand dollars thus escaping the law which they themselves placed upon the statute books. That is an iniquitous policy. The policy which we have heard announced to-day, that to the victors belong the spoils is also a vicious system. It came to us from the American side of the line and it is practised in Canada just as strongly and just as openly as it is in the country of its origin.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows I did not lay down any such doctrine.
tMr. CAMPBELL. It is refreshing to hear the member for Dufferin (Mr. Barr) protesting against the spoils system. He says this government has dismissed a great many officials, but let him look around the cities of Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal at the hundreds of officials in the Customs, the Inland Revenue, and Post Office, and he cannot point to a single man who has been dismissed except for cause. Offensive partisanship or inefficiency has been proved in each case after investigation. Let the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barr) take his advice to his friends in Toronto. Mr. Whitney does not hold a court of investigation and ask for evidence ; he chops off the heads [DOT]of Liberal officials. Every license commissioner in the whole province of Ontario almost has been dismissed without cause, and every license inspector has been dismissed.
No.
Nearly every one of them. In West York, East York, North York and in Kent these officials were dismissed and no investigation held.
Will you say they were dismissed without cause ? Will you say as the representative of Centre York that the license inspectors did their duty ?

Yes, I will. In East and West York the license inspectors were most efficient men and men who had not taken any part in politics since their appointment several years ago. Mr. Russel in East York is one of the most highly respected men in the county ; lie is a man who had studiously avoided taking part in politics and yet his head has been cut off without investigation or inquiry. In West York it is the same. For the few months Mr. Whitney has been in power he has dismissed hundreds of officials all over the province. The fishery overseers have gone also and all without an investigation. Mr. Whitney is fresh at the business yet ; he is making good headway so far, and if he continues I venture to say there will be very few Liberal officials in Ontario in a short while. Are we squealing or whining about it V For the last ten years these gentlemen opposite have been whining and squealing because officials have been dismissed for offensive partisanship, but it is time they let up on that and turned their attention to their friends in Toronto who are doing ten times worse. Possibly there may be one official out of hundreds who has been dismissed, but I can tell you that the course pursued by this government in this respect reflects the highest credit on them. To these gentlemen opposite I say : go and talk to Mr. Whitney as you are talking here and it may do some good.
It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to talk generally, but I challenge him to put his finger on a single license inspector who has been dismised without cause.
East and W7est York and Kent.

In East and WTest York they were bitter partisans and if they had not been dismissed it would have been a disgrace to the government. In the first place they did nothing to carry out the law. We all know that the license commissioners are only appointed from year to year.
I refer to license inspectors.

Yes, they allowed the gambling hells to operate and they let the hotels

keep open at all hours In that part of the country.
They did not.

I speak from what I know, and I say that they did nothing but draw their salaries. In Dufferin we have the same inspector, but the commissioners were changed and I can assure you that the change was a great improvement. The inspectors that have not been removed for cause now know that they have to do their duty, and that if they do not they will be dismissed. Every day there are cases brought up in this House where good officials have been dismissed for no reason whatever. I have myself pointed out that in my own county a postmaster after seven years service was dismissed without any cause except that ' he was a Conservative and exercised his franchise.

I am astonished to hear the member for Dufferin (Mr. Barr) make such statements in this House; I challenge him to give the name of one man in the large county of Wellington who has been dismissed by this government on account of polities. The hon. gentleman knows very well that we had a great many civil servants in Wellington who were strong partisans. It is astonishing to me that a man of as high standing as the hon. member for Dufferin would make such statements. In the province of Ontario there has scarcely been a man removed from the position he occupied in 1896 for such cause as the hon. gentleman has mentioned. I challenge him to name one man who has been removed for that cause in the large and populous county of Wellington, which contains the city of Guelph ; but I can name several Conservatives who have been appointed or reappointed to good positions in that county.
Give us the names of the ones reinstated.
I will give the hon. gentleman not only the names *of those reinstated, but the names of those appointed. I will give him the names privately.

What we object to is that these men are breaking the law, which is that they must take tenders if the amount is over $5,000. They are breaking the law by doing such work by day's work, and they are using that day's work to make votes; that is the sum and substance of the whole thing ; and after the announcement made by the minister to-day, we understand why they are breaking the law. It the law makers are to be law breakers, what is the country coming to ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend cannot undei stand why they are breaking the law, Mr. BARR.
because as a matter of fact they are not breaking it.

With reference to the dismissal of officials, the Toronto 1 Telegram ' a Conservative paper, some time ago urged the Whitney government not to dismiss Liberal officials from office, saying that the Laurier government in that respect had set a good example.

I am sure the Minister of Finance regards the incident in connection with the Port Arthur dredging with as much regret as any man in this House. In order to avoid any such irregularity in

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think each transaction must be defended on its own merits. I am informed that the hon. gentleman is mistaken when he says that it was necessary to inspect the plans and specifications. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If one wants to come to the department to get more information he is free to do so. The statement is made to me that the information in the advertisement was sufficient to enable a man to tender. I think the time was extended in the case referred to.
