speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that it would have been.

I know that the Minister of Finance will not defend such a transaction, and if he acknowledges, as I think he will honestly acknowledge that there was no defence in this case, then I ask him if it would not be wise to fix some minimum time between the notice and the opening of the tenders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that any rule can be laid down except the general one that reasonable and sufficient notice should be given in every case where the government invites tenders.
That was the rule before but it was not respected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It often happens that for some good reason it is found that the time is too short and that it has to be extended. I agree with the hon. gentleman that reasonable and sufficient notice should be given, but if he asks me to specify the number of days I would like to reserve judgment on that.
Would the hon. gentleman say that the minimum time should be ten or twenty days ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is better to allow each transaction to stand on its own merits. It is enough to say there should be a fair and reasonable notice that will give every man within reasonable distance an opportunity of tendering.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
In the Port Arthur case the time was only extended when attention was called to it in parliament, and the case was so indefensible that the Minister of Public Works had to back down and extend the time. The advertisement in that case was dated on the 7th of April, it was first published on the 11th and tenders were to be opened on the 14th so that there were only 3 days for the public to tender. It went further than that: the dredge had to be owned by a person in Canada, it had to be on the ground on the 20th of April before the ice was out of the harbour where the work was to be done, there was no allowance for towing and there was only one dredge in that locality which was partly owned by a member of this House. The government should learn from that instance that a reasonable time should' be specified so that the public money may not be given

away to political friends as was clearly the intention in this case.
Now, with reference to the Grand river dredging, the item under discussion, the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) was obliged to leave this afternoon, and as there is not going to be a vote in the main estimates or further supplementary estimates for this work I will either have to ask the item to stand or else get the promise of the Finance Minister that when the Ontario estimates are being discussed the hon. member for Haldimand will have an opportunity to make the remarks he intended to make on this vote. This is another Conmee-Bowman job as I understand from my friend (Mr. Lalor). This work was done by a dredge owned by Mr. Bowman, and I believe that several hundred dollars were allowed him for towing this dredge from the mouth of the Grand river to Dunnville besides the handsome price paid him for the work. No wonder that the appropriation of last year is overrun by some $6,000 if the statements made by my hon. friend from Haldimand are correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite agree that if the hon. gentleman from Haldimand desires to say anything on this matter, that on the general vote for dredging in Ontario he should have the opportunity for a free discussion. If there is reason to believe that there is anything wrong in the expenditure I would suggest to my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) that some of these days when the Public Accounts Committee meets, the matter be taken up.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The trouble is that this money is being spent this year and we cannot get it before the Public Accounts Committee, but you will hear about it next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Wait till you see us next year.

I have here the advertisement with reference to the Port Arthur dredging as it appeared in the Toronto ' Globe ' of April the 11th, 1905. It says :
Plans showing where dredging is to be performed can he seen in the office of the chief engineer of the department, where also any additional information required can be obtained.
If the Finance Minister looks at the advertisement he will see that no specifications are given and that it does not even say where the work is to be done. In fact it invites tenderers to go to the Public Works Department to get information. This very incident makes it most important that some fixed time should be provided. A minimum time should be fixed and that minimum time should be ample to allow all persons who desire to tender for work of this kind, a proper opportunity to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think there was an earlier advertisement which contained no information on that subject.

That is the advertisement we quarrelled about.
Mr. FIELDING, I think the hon. gentleman's quarrel was with the lack of time and not the lack of information.

That was one of the principal grounds of complaint, that it only gave three days' time for an intending contractor to ascertain at what part of Port Arthur harbour the dredging was to be done, the character of the dredging and the conditions prevailing. Then, if an examination of the ground was necessary, he would have had to use a flying machine to get there, and then to cut through two feet of solid ice in order to ascertain what the bottom of the harbour was like, and then be back here with his tender, all within the space of three days. The effect of that was Simply to eliminate from competition everything except the Conmee & Bowman dredges, which were ice-bound in Port Arthur harbour, and these dredges alone could perform that work. Another fact was brought forcibly to the attention of the government, the extraordinarily significant fact that no allowance was made for towing, whereas in other contracts as high as $1,500 had been allowed for towing plant to the scene of operations. That certainly was not conducive to any tenderers other than Conmee & Bowman, or the owners of the dredges then in the harbour. It was the first advertisement that was complained of and which the hon. member for Peel has cited. That advertisement, the hon. gentleman must admit, contains no such information as he thought a little while ago it did contain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was informed the first advertisement did contain such information. However, that is not the point in question ; it is the time that is under discussion, and if three days only were allowed, I think that insufficient. I understand the real point of grievance was the time, and I quite admit that three days is not sufficient notice for such work.

Does the hon. gentleman not now think it is high time, when irregularities so grave occur in connection with a contract involving $195,000 expenditure, that a principle was laid down, and that the government should say : We will not allow a work of this kind to be awarded except after advertisement for ten days or two weeks, so that the public will know the minimum amount of advertising that will be allowed by the department ? Surely it is not unreasonable to ask this. If this thing had not been brought to the attention of the government on April 13, the day before these tenders were closed, contracts involv-

tag $195,000 of public money would have been let practically without any opportunity of tendering, and without intending contractors having an opportunity even of knowing that tenders were invited, and, if they did know, they could only tender in the dark, because they could not tell from the advertisement what the conditions were there without coming to Ottawa to inspect these plans and specifications, and probably they might have been told when they came to Ottawa that they would have to go to Port Arthur to inspect the bottom of the lake in order to verify the conditions shown in the plans. The hon. gentleman admits that the time is too short. Will he say now that not a contract shall be let except on such and such notice, or will he stick to the principle that reasonable time shall be allowed ? That was the principle in vogue before the Port Arthur grievance was raised. The 'Minister of Public Works said that was the principle on which these contracts were let, that reasonable time should be allowed, and this he considered a reasonable time. If that was the principle of the department before this irregularity was brought to the attention of the government, surely it is not unreasonable to ask the government now to change it and stipulate that at least a certain number of days, to be increased according to the importance of the contract and the distance to a longer time, shall be allowed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not agree that any good purpose could be served by stipulating a specific number of days. I would be quite prepared to agree that ten days' notice would be little enough for a work of this kind, and that it would be better to have longer notice, but I would not be prepared to lay down a minimum time. I think the matter will have to be left to what is fair and reasonable ; and if that is not done, my hon. friends will certainly not fail to remind us of it. Meantime, I promised the hon. member for Lennox to confirm a statement I made as to a certain appropriation having been made. I presume from his having left the chamber that he did not consider it important, but it will be found on page 42 of the Supply Bill.
Collingwood harbour, $50,000.

speechtext: This is for unpaid accounts for dredging performed by C. S. Boone, by dredges Nos. 10 and 14, in channel, to 24 feet depth, and some cribwork, steps, &c. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We will discuss it then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Whitby harbour-dredging, $4,050.

speechtext: The appropriation in that case was $10,000, and a further sum of $4,050 was required to complete the payments. The dredge ' Trenton,' owned by Contractor R. Weddell, operated from August 17 to November 14, 1904, the close of navigation. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: $14,050 has been spent ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The work is done.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It certainly seems to me that these over-expenditures are extremely large this year in nearly every instance. The elections certainly must have had something to do with the over-expenditures. I do not know by what right the government asks for $50,000 to make certain improvements and then spends $100,000 without consulting parliament. I think that when the amount voted is exhausted the work should stop until parliament meets again and the government can ask for another vote, instead of -taking carte blanche to spend as much money as they like. I think the government should ask what they require for the year, and parliament will cheerfully vote it if, in their opinion, the work should be done. I do not think the government should say : We asked for $50,000, but we had an election and spent $100,000, and therefore must have another $50,000.
Was the Collingwood contract completed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The contractor was O. S. Boone, and the work was done on the basis of so much per yard-$2.30 for rock and $1.40 for hard-pan.

I notice that last year tills matter was pretty fully discussed, and the minister, Mr. Hyman, said :
The total amount of the contract is $87,000, we paid on that $49,000, and this is to complete the balance of the work.
What the committtee would like to know is whether the contract referred to by the minister at that time has been completed, and if so, what amount is unpaid on it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The engineers inform me that the contract there referred to was finished, and that afterwards additional work was authorized at the same rates, so as to widen the channel.

That does not answer the point. The minister of last year stated that the work for which $50,000 was to be appropriated was let by tender, and that the contract was for $87,000. What the committee would like to know is whether that contract has been completed. The minister now says that the work has been done at so much per cubic yard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand that that contract was completed in the manner stated; that the work was extended at the rates I have mentioned, which are the equivalent of the contract price ; and that as respects any additional work, tenders have now been called for a further contract.
Sault Ste. Marie-harbour improvements, including dredging of approaches-balances due on contract work, &c., $25,000.
What is this work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This work was done by contract by Mr. Joseph Battle, of Thorold. Ontario. The amount of the contract was $65,000, and there was extra work authorized to the amount of $1,200, with charges for superintendence and contingencies, bringing the whole amount up to $68,700, of which $43,659.22 has been paid, and the balance of $25,000 in round numbers is still to be paid.
Will the hon. gentleman state what the nature of the work was, what the extras were, and who was the per son employed to superintend the work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The officer who inspected the work was Mr. Boyd. He is not regularly in the employ of the government, but was employed for that purpose.
Is the hon gentleman aware that Mr. Boyd is employed as wharfinger at Sault Ste. Marie at a regular salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know what the custom is there, but usually wharfingers are not paid salaries, but are allowed a percentage of their receipts, not exceeding 25 per cent in the Marine Department, and they are not commonly regarded as salaried officials.

With regard to the superintendent, the result would be that while that work was going on, Mr. Boyd would be sitting in his office, attending to his business as wharfinger, and occasionally inspecting this work. He would De getting the same fees as wharfinger whether he acted as superintendent or not. His time as wharfinger is supposed to be exclusively given to the government, while, as a matter of fact, his time would be divided between his duties as wharfinger and his duties as superintendent of this work. In short, he gets double pay for doing work that would require constant and exclusive attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose that if a past-master getting a few dollars a year in a small country post office were employed under similar conditions, we would be told that he was paid two salaries. I think the allowance made to wharfingers, unless the business is very large, is not contemplated as calling for a man's whole time. It is a small percentage on the amount he collects.
The hon. gentleman has not stated the nature of the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The stem of the old wharf, formerly called Plummer's wharf, was lengthened by adding 250 feet in length, 60 feet in width and from 25 to 31 feet in height, and a wing turned up stream 250 feet in length, 50 feet in width, and from 31 to 33 feet in height. The top stands 6| feet above low water.
Is that all the work for which this appropriation is required ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
What is the dredging that is included ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no dredging in this. The word * dredging ' is a part of the heading of the first appropriation, and they copied the same words.

I refer the hon. gentleman to page 5627 of ' Hansard ' where he will find a number of questions and answers concerning the government docks at Sault Ste. Marie. In question 12, I asked who was the wharfinger employed during the construction of the extension of the dock and at what rate was he paid, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries replied that the wharfinger appointed by that department was retained in office, that his name is George A. Boyd, and that he was paid at the rate of $142 per month during the season of navigation out of the fees collected by him, and further that the wharfinger paid for all necessary assistance. Well, this extension work was done during the season of navigation. By question 10,
I asked under whose immediate local supervision was this extension work performed, and the minister replied that it was performed under the supervision of George A. Boyd, at $3 per day. Therefore this same man was getting $142 per month and $3 per day at the same time. What was the total period during which this man Boyd was paid for superintending that work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give the information. The usual practice is to pay these wharfingers by fees, and I was dealing with the usual practice, having no special knowledge of the amount of business done at that wharf.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would depend on the amount of business. It seems to be very considerable, and his fees would amount to a considerable sum. The Public Works Department might not have any knowledge of the fact tnat he was acting as wharfinger. I presume it is the same man.
It is said to be the same man.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it so stated in the answer to the question ?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I presume the hon. gentleman knows that it is the same man when he says so ?
I know it is the same and a very useful man in an election.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is an additional virtue.

No doubt that was the great factor in giving him this $3 per day extra. An election was imminent in that constituency. A great deal of money was spent and a great many votes created, and created in a manner -which will yet have to be brought to the attention of this House, and which forms one of the greatest election scandals ever perpetrated in the Dominion. Votes were created absolutely without law or reason or any reasonable excuse at all in that district of West Algoma. 543 votes were put upon the voters' list in a single day without notice to anybody, and this Mr. George A. Boyd, who was not required to give his whole time to his duties as wharfinger and got $3 per day besides as superintendent, was the agent who was exceedingly active on behalf of the Liberal candidate. No doubt this was his reward. I wonder shall he be dealt with in the same severe manner as the Postmaster General dealt with the postmaster at Kentvale. Men were brought in on trains to my knowledge in parties of from six to eight to vote for the Liberal candidate in the January election. This same gentleman was very active on behalf of this government in the Dominion election and on behalf of the Ontario government in the provincial election.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose that since all these different things happened in that election, the hon. gentleman will use the machinery provided by parliament for investigating them ? I take it for granted he has appealed to the courts to have this thing straightened out ?

I am glad the hon. gentleman brings that up. If he looks at the public accounts, he will see that it must have cost this country several hundreds of dollars to employ counsel to resist the demand for a writ of prohibition which I made at the moment this outrage was committed. If he will consult Judge Meredith's decision, delivered shortly before the election, he will see that the judge held that the extraordinary Order in Council was not to be followed, by which this government proposed to make voters' lists in violation of every statute in Ontario. That is what was done and that is on record, and that record will be laid before this House. It was fortunately not necessary to go into the election court, but it may be necessary to ask parliament to refer the matter to the Privileges and Elections Committee. 543 names were created in that district illegally, without any excuse, with

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I would ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) if the attention of the Attorney General of Ontario has been called to these outrages, and if so, what that officer is doing ?

I do not know whether the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) was in the House a little while ago or not. But I may tell him that the attention of the courts have been called to the matter. And I may tell him that three counsel were employed and paid by this government, and 1 suppose that a reasonable amount will appear in the public accounts for their services. X would remind the Minister of Finance of that, there is very interesting reading in the judgment. And I would commend that judgment also to the hon. member for Centre York (Mr. Campbell) together with the facts on which it proceeded. I was struck with the virtue shown by the hon. gentleman in commenting on certain matters before we rose at six o'clock. If he will study the facts in connection for the application for prohibition in respect to the West Algoma voters' lists during October last, he will find interesting reading and may have reason to change the view as to the absence of the virtue of every action of this government.

speechtext: Why build wharfs up there ?

speechtext: Because we wish to be fair to all parts of the country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have urged upon the government for many years to be fair to the district in the St. Lawrence, the township of Howe island which is thickly settled with farmers, principally lower Canadians who settled there many years ago. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ferries and bridges would rightly come within our jurisdiction but wharfs are our legitimate business.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
There are about a dozen wharfs around this Howe island but all built by the people. At my urgent request the government has promised again and again to look into the building of a wharf there, but it has not been done. The Dominion government control the river there, but Mr. TAYLOR.
they will not build a bridge to connect the island with the mainland.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A bridge within the limits of a province, is ordinarily considered a provincial work. An inter-provincial bridge sometimes has claims upon the Dominion, but an ordinary highway bridge entirely within the province would be considered a local -work. Of course, it is not always easy to lay down the line between local and Dominion authority, but I think the definition I give, so far as it goes, is correct.
Georgian bay and Pointe au Baril route-improvement of the Devil's Elbow channel between Parry Sound and Kilarney $750.

This is the last item of the Ontario group. I desire to call the attention of the committee to the fact that there is nothing in these supplementary estimates for Toronto harbour. This is a matter which has been again and again brought up in this House, by the late Mr. Clarke and also by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) and the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp). The necessity for the work is beyond question. The government engineers have, from time to time so certified. The particular work to which I refer is the straightening of the River Don and the dredging of the harbour. When the main estimates were under consideration the attention of the minister was called to this work and he promised to take the matter into consideration. Since that time a deputation consisting of the mayor and others from the city of Toronto have waited upon the Minister of Public Works and made out what appears to be a very good case for an appropriation for this work. The minister again on that occasion promised to consider it, and the deputation were led to believe that something would be done, or at least considered. Now the supplementary estimates are completed and nothing appears. From year to year, in the past, amounts have appeared in the estimates for this work, but the work has never been done and the money has never been expended. I desire to warn the government now that Toronto harbour is a government work the same as Quebec, Halifax or any other, and the harbour is rapidly filling up for want of dredging. Material is carried down in large quantities by the River Don and deposited in the harbour. It is estimated by the government's own engineer that enough silt sufficient to cover five acres to the depth of 10 feet is deposited in the harbour every year by the action of the River Don. The result is that the eastern part of the harbour is no longer a harbour-it has ceased to be one. The slips in the eastern part of the harbour are

kept open, where they are kept open at all, by dredging carried on by the city council and the harbour commissioners of Toronto. The government has spent no money on that work. The work will have to be undertaken some day and it will cost a great deal of money because of the delay which has taken place. I had hoped that these supplementary estimates would contain some appropriation for that work. However, if the supplementary estimates are not all down I hope the government will consider the matter and the Minister of Public Works will give it the consideration he promised the deputation should be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimates we have under consideration, I would remind my hon. friend, are only for the fiscal year which has now nearly expired-they are simply to close the transactions of the year. The appropriations for the coming year do not appear in these estimates. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. C. Macdonell) will turn to the main estimates for the fiscal year beginning 1st .Tuly next, he, will see considerable appropriations for Toronto harbour. I am aware of the fact referred to Jjy the minister. But these works are entirely different from the one to which I refer. The work I refer to is the straightening of the River Don and the dredging of the main harbour. Now that the hon. minister has mentioned those works I think it only right to say that although they were provided for in the original estimates the contract is not yet let. speechtext:
The Ottawa river is the dividing line between two great provinces, and the bridge there is an interprovincial bridge. This is somewhat different front a bridge entirely within the province.

000.

speechtext: She is approaching completion now, and will likely be finished in a short time.
Where is she being built ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At the government shipyards, Sorel.
Where will the ' W. S. Fielding ' be placed at work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter which is still not decided. I do not know whether it is the dredge or the name but there are numerous applicants for her.

When the construction of this dredge was being provided for, I believe the Minister of Public Works stated that she would be able to do some work at St. John harbour. It requires a special kind of dredge to do the work there and the then Minister of Public Works stated that this dredge would be suitable for that work and that she would be sent to St. John harbour when completed. Is that still the intention of the department ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not the intention to regard this dredge as being built for any particular place ; it is built for service in the maritime provinces generally and it certainly would be capable of doing the work at St. John. I understand, however, that other provision is being made for certain dredging at St. John harbour, which will not require the services of this dredge.
I am aware of that. Can the minister say what action has been already taken with regard to that other dredge to which he refers ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There have been some negotiations which I think are intended to make provision for the work which the hon. gentleman and I have in mind. How ever, it has not yet been finally arranged, although it is likely to be arranged very shortly.
Does the minister think it will be arranged early enough to have the work done this season.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The quantity of dredging there is very considerable and I do not imagine it will all be completed this season. I would not like to be too definite, because it is a matter which has engaged the attention of the Minister of Public Works and except in a general way I am not familiar with it.
WThat is the cost of the 'King Edward' that is being built by the Poisons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: According to the information furnished me it will cost $220,000.
Was the contract let by tender ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Was the construction of the dredge which is being built by the Bertram Company let by tender ?
'Mr. FIELDING. Yes.
How many tenders were put in for these two dredges, and by whom ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The deputy informs me that speaking from memory he thinks three tenders -were put in, all from Toronto firms. There are only a few people in Canada who can do work of that character.
I am aware of that.
Is it the intention of the government to do any dredging in the St. John river this year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a dredge engaged in the St. John river every year and I think she will he continued this year.

I directed the attention of the Minister of Public Works to some dredging which is necessary to do on the Washdemoali river, one of the tributaries of the St. John. It is a very important and necessary work and would not be very costly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was there not some dredging done there last year ?

Yes, there was some dredging done in front of the wharf and it has been found very useful. The work I speak of is required in the channel of the river, and it is situated at a point near where there are quite a number of people living. The vessels that ply along the coast have too large a draught to be able to navigate there under present conditions without unloading part of their cargo, which of course, causes great inconvenience as well as loss of money. I have already drawn the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the matter and he informed me that he would direct his engineer to make a report. I ask now if the engineer has acted on the minister's instructions ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will see that a note is taken of the request made by my hon. friend (Mr. Wilmot) and I will draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to it. I am not able to give any information as to that point at present.

I wish also to draw the attention of the government to the fact that there are several points on the main river St. John which ought to be attended to. I have complained to this government and also to the Conservative government, that I never saw a Minister of the Public Works or any of the chiefs of the department visit the St. John river which is one of the chief rivers in the Dominion. The ,ministers seem to depend altogether on the opinion of the local officers, and I would earnestly urge on the government and on the Public Works Department that they should pay more attention to that important river.
Telegraph lines, Qu'Apelie, Edmonton and Moosejaw, (Wood Mountain section), $4,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Parliament was not consulted about this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Matters arise occasionally on which it is necessary to take action without waiting to consult parliament.
Did this arise with the American government ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the commission was at the instance of the American government ?

What Is this for ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The business of the country is increasing, and a larger staff is required.
What was the amount voted last year for that branch ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We were passing estimates in July or August last year, and the government must have known how much it would take to run that staff for the balance of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend must remember that while parliament did not prorogue until August, ihe estimates were prepared long before that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: But an engineer, if he is competent should be able to estimate within a few dollars what it would cost to run his department for the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In proportion to the total expenditure the excess is not very large.
When the minister of a department goes before Council and asks for money, does not the Minister of Finance ask questions to find out whether the expenditure is necessary or not ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes.

More than that, the Minister of Finance used to cut out some expenditures and act as if he. had charge of the treasury of the country. There is no doubt that we are voting very large amounts of money that should have been thought of when the main estimates were made up. There seems to be a lack of business management on the part of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not sure that some of these votes are not due to the fact that the Minister of Finance is apt to be stingy and to try to cut down some of the estimates ; for the minister affected comes Mr. FIELDING.
back at the end of the year and says, you would not give it to me at the beginning of the year, and I must have it now.

speechtext: Over the Canadian Pacific Railway to points in the Territories, 50 cents for ten words. On messages from here we have to pay the Canadian Pacific Railway rates from Qu'Appelle.

How much did it cost altogether ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: This $43,000 is all for working expenses ?

speechtext: How much is taken in the main estimates ?

speechtext:
$183,000. We are asking $43,000 more.
Mr. TAYLOR, Who does the disbursing or the keeping of the accounts of this Yukon line ? Is it Mr. Charleson ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No ; he was employed on the construction. This comes under the general supervision of the officer in charge of our telegraph service at Ottawa, Mr. Keeley.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How comes it that he asked for $183,000 last year and now wants $41,000 more ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The old arrears on maintenance have something to do with this.
What do the repairs cost each year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not that information just now, but will get it later on. The repairs are done by our own officials, and are included in the general charge of maintenance.
This looks a very large item for a newly constructed line.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been running six years.

Is not that the line which a company offered to build for nothing and to carry besides government messages free ? Was not that shown by the correspondence between 'Mr. Blair and some English company when it was taken out of his hands by Mr. Tarte and built at the expense of the government ? Now, it has cost over $700,000, and there is a deficit on it every year of $50,000.	-	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would not follow that the company which made the proposal would have been able to do the good things they promised. Companies are usually generous in their offers: Mr. Tarte's view was that the construction of this line was of great importance to Canada, and that we could not afford to let it go into the hands of a company, which might not maintain it efficiently.
To pay J. C. TachS for special services as district superintendent of telegraphs at Chicoutimi from January 1 to June 30, 1905, $150.

speechtext:
His regular salary is $1,750, and he is allowed these $300 extra for this service, increasing his salary to $2,050. He could not get an increase according to his rank without a special vote, and that is why it is done in this way.
Franchise Act-to complete cost of voters' lists for election of 1904, $10,000 ; new edition of Electoral Atlas, $3,500 ;	$13,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When this item was up before I was asked one or two questions with regard to the electoral atlas that is being printed.
Will that be distributed to members before the end of the election ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The King's Printer says he is not quite sure that it will be completed before the end of the session but it is distributed to the members. I was asked whether the lists under the Franchise Act vs'ere printed every year. It is not the practice to print these every year although the Act may seem to contemplate that, but the custom is to print them at any time when there is an expectation of an election.

A few days ago the Printing Committee had the pleasure of visiting the Printing Bureau and through the courtesy of Dr. Dawson and his assistants we were shown everything that could be seen there. I wish to call the attention of the minister to the inadequacy of the space in that building. It is entirely too small for the work done there and I think the public service would have better results if the establishment was enlarged so that all the printing for the public service could be done there. Take the printing of the lists. That is an immense work and that
building I think should be at least double the size it is to-day. As we are spending a lot of money-my hon. friend speaks of the growing time

I think money voted for that purpose would be usefully spent and although the building was enlarged last year the enlargement is hardly noticeable, it is so small. The government have a good deal of ground there and I think it would be good policy to enlarge the place as soon as possible. If my hon. friend asks the opinion of Dr. Dawson he will be convinced that the sooner that is done the better.
Mr. [DOT] W. J. ROCHE. I presume when the lists are sent down from the various provinces, they come direct to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery and he sends them to the King's Printer to have them printed.
I	do not suppose that after they are printed from the original copy they come under the supervision of the King's Printer himself. There are certain proof-readers no doubt, but what I wish to draw to the attention of the Finance Minister is in connection with the lists for Manitoba for the last election. There were a great many typographical errors; in fact so many that there was a suspicion in the minds of many of my own friends that they were not at all accidental. Of course I am not blaming the King's Printer for this, but some of my supporters desired me to bring it up in the House, because they thought some person, possibly in the printing office, must have been tampering with them and that an arrangement existed. For instance in the particular district where I reside, there was a list of 11 names shown to me. All these
II	names were typographical errors ; instead of being put down as residing in 15-16, they were put in 16-17. This gave a good excuse to the officers who prepared the list for scoring these men off their own township and many of them had to travel many miles from their own township although their own polls were within a mile or two of their homes and when they got to these other polls perhaps ten or fifteen miles away, they found their names had not been transferred. Out of these 11 names 10 were Conservative, and the only one that was a Liberal was not scored off. I thought I would bring this up because really there were a great many errors of this character in connection .with the printing of the municipal list in our province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These errors are most annoying and it is very difficult to give any explanation of such a statement as the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) has mentioned. But I am assured by the King's Printer it is hardly possible that there should be any intention of any wrong-doing in the matter. The lists are

read very carefully, or should be, by capable proof-readers, by reliable men who have been in the service of the department a great many years, and the King's Printer feels the utmost confidence in their good intentions. If the error has occurred some one is to blame.
Their eyesight is failing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are not as young as they used to be, but it is hardly possible they could have any conception of who the people up there were.
Unless there was some one to post them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is still more difficult of conception.	'
It is quite possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If any one was unfair enough to do it they would hardly go to the Printing Bureau and no one there would permit such a thing to be done. It is a blunder and it is unfortunate it has happened, but it is hardly possible it could be done by design. It is carelessness, but I am sure it is an accident.

It is strange It
should be confined to the one party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The King's Printer has never had it brought to his notice before and has had no opportunity of investigating it.

On the question of expenditure for printing voters' lists it steems to me that	an arrangement
could be entered into between the Dominion government and the local governments that would avoid the expenditure of such a large amount of money for printing Dominion lists. The minister will keep in mind the fact that the list used, in Ontario for example, for the local is the same as for the Dominion. These lists are printed every year by the mun'clpal'.t'es and are used for the municipal elections and used as well for the provincial election when it is held every four years. I cannot understand why an agreement should not be entered into between the government of Canada and the local governments so that the list as printed by the municipalities, which is after all the list used in the election, should not be used without being sent to Ottawa to be printed at all. We have these lists printed every year and it seems to me a useless expenditure of money that the very same names should be transmitted to Ottawa, printed in new form and sent back to the different constituencies when they are already in printed form.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The suggestion is worthy of consideration. I am inclined to Mr. FIELDING.
think the provincial or municipal printing of lists is not so general as my hon. friend thinks. He is particularly speaking no doubt from his own observation in Ontario. I think I am correct in stating that in some province the municipalities do not print their lists. I know I have seen in rural districts, written lists posted up and I dare say the municipalities jirould_not care to incur the expense of printing. If it would be possible to bring about harmonious action between the Dominion, provincial and municipal authorities there might be much convenience. I am not advised as to whether it is possible to arrange this.

In Quebec the lists are not printed, but I do not see if they are printed in Ontario that there is any use in doing it a second time. The lists might be printed in provinces or municipalities where they are not printed. The printing of lists in Ontario, where there are 90 counties, is a useless expense.

There is one feature connected with the printing of the lists to which I would call attention, that is the form in which the lists are got up. Would it not be possible to have them made up in a form more convenient for the use of candidates and others ? Of course it may be more convenient for the Printing Bureau to get them out in long sheets, but they are rather inconvenient for handling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The printing in blank form would be convenient for the candidates and the public certainly. But it would involve more cost and more time in the printing.
Were many of the lists preparatory to the last Dominion elections printed outside ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: About forty of them. The details are given in the report of the King's printer.
Does the minister know what provinces they represented ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were mainly of Ontario and Quebec constituencies.
Were they printed in one particular newspaper office V

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were scattered among a number of offices. -
Liberal, I suppose ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No doubt. The others would not do work for this wicked government.

Unprovided items, 1903-4-To cover unprovided items, 1903-4, as per Auditor General's Report, page C-4, $280,551.40.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is not an appropriation of money, tout a mere formal vote which the Auditor General likes to have at the close of the year'to wind up the accounts. It arises in this way : Appropriations are made to the department for the different 'branches of its business. It sometimes happens that the minister, the accountants and the Auditojr General do not exactly agree as to the particular manner in which charges should he made. For instance, the minister has an expenditure charged in one way ; the Auditor General makes up his mind that he will charge it against another. The result is that one particular branch is exceeded while in the other there is an excess. This is not an authority for the payment of a dollar, but the Auditor General has asked that a formal appropriation he made in this way to wind up the accounts.
